title: The diffraction grating

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Recall and use d sin θ = nλ for a diffraction grating, and describe how a diffraction grating is used to determine the wavelength of light.

blocks.heading: The grating equation
blocks.text: A diffraction grating is a slide carrying many equally spaced parallel slits — several hundred to a few thousand per millimetre. Its maxima sit at angles given by d sin θ = nλ, where d is the spacing between the centres of neighbouring slits in m, θ the angle between the straight-through direction and the nth-order maximum, n the order of the maximum, and λ the wavelength in m. The order counts the maxima out from the centre: n = 0 is the straight-through maximum, n = 1 the first on either side, and at the nth-order maximum the path difference between waves from neighbouring slits is n whole wavelengths — so the displacements arriving from neighbouring slits, each point's distance from its rest position, are in step and add. The spacing is the reciprocal of the line density: for N lines per millimetre, convert to lines per metre first, then d = 1 ÷ N. Because sin θ cannot exceed 1, the largest order visible is the greatest whole number n with n ≤ d ÷ λ.

blocks.heading: Worked example: the first order of green light
blocks.text: Green light of wavelength 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m falls normally on a grating with 400 lines per mm. Line density: N = 400 per mm = 4.00 × 10⁵ per m, so d = 1 ÷ N = 2.50 × 10⁻⁶ m. Equation for the first order: sin θ = nλ ÷ d. Substitution: sin θ = (1 × 5.0 × 10⁻⁷) ÷ (2.50 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.20. So θ = 11.5° to three significant figures. Because the angle is modest, the maxima of the first order sit near the centre of the screen; a grating with more lines per mm gives a larger angle and a more precise measurement of θ.

blocks.heading: Finding a wavelength with a grating
blocks.text: To determine a wavelength, shine the light normally onto the grating and let the pattern fall on a screen a measured distance away. Measure the distance from the central maximum to the chosen order's bright line, together with the grating-to-screen distance; the tangent of the angle is their ratio, giving θ. The line density printed on the grating mount gives d = 1 ÷ N with N converted to lines per metre. Then the equation λ = (d sin θ) ÷ n gives the wavelength. A grating is preferred to a double slit because its maxima are sharper and brighter, and its larger angles carry a smaller percentage uncertainty, so the wavelength comes out more precise. The structure of any mounting apparatus is a laboratory matter; the physics needed at this level is the geometry of the angles and the one equation.

blocks.heading: White light through a grating
blocks.text: White light is a mixture of wavelengths, and d sin θ = nλ sends each wavelength to its own angle. At the centre all wavelengths share θ = 0, so the central maximum stays white. In each outer order the colours separate: violet, the shortest visible wavelength of about 4 × 10⁻⁷ m, is deviated least and sits nearest the centre; red, about 7 × 10⁻⁷ m, is deviated most and sits outermost. Each order is therefore a band of colours, and the bands repeat at larger angles for the higher orders.

blocks.heading: d is a spacing in metres; θ is measured from the centre
blocks.text: Two slips recur with the grating equation. First, d is the slit spacing in metres, not the number of lines: for a 500-lines-per-mm grating, N = 5.00 × 10⁵ per m and d = 1 ÷ N = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m; substituting 500 puts the equation out by many powers of ten. Second, θ is measured from the straight-through direction to the maximum concerned: the angle between the two first-order maxima, one on each side, is 2θ. The test: is d a spacing in metres, and is θ measured from the centre?

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The grating is the many-slit version of the double slit of 8.3: its maxima are interference maxima, sharpened by the many slits. The geometry of the angles continues the trigonometry of topic 1, and the wavelengths it separates come from the regions of the spectrum met in topic 7.
